paras: The stoning of John H. Harris was an attack on a Black Democratic campaign speaker from Virginia at New Castle, Delaware, on the night of Saturday, July 31, 1880, when missiles were thrown at him from a crowd as he spoke outside the courthouse. The stone missed Harris but severely wounded a white bystander, and Harris spent the night under the sheriff's protection. Delaware papers attributed the attack to Black listeners opposed to a Black man speaking for the Democrats, and Democratic papers across the country used it as an answer to Republican reports of Southern outrages.

Harris, a colored man claiming to come from Virginia, arrived in Wilmington in late July 1880 to organize colored Hancock and English clubs. According to the Smyrna Times, he had collected $25 or $30 from Democratic officials, while the Bel Air Argyle in Maryland called him "an undoubted swindler." The same paper wrote that the Jefferson Club had snubbed him because the Delaware Democracy was "a white man's party."

On Saturday evening Harris went to New Castle to speak and found the courthouse closed. A crowd of 300 or 400, "mostly blacks" in the Wilmington Every Evening account, gathered in front of the building, and Harris spoke from a carriage whose horse had been unhitched. As he urged the Black listeners to vote the Democratic ticket, some grew restless and "mutterings were heard."

After nearly half an hour a stone of about a pound (a brick, in the Smyrna Times and the State Journal) came from the crowd, missed Harris and struck a white man named McNulty on the head; smaller stones followed, and the sheriff began summoning a posse comitatus.

Harris spoke a little longer and withdrew, and his frightened driver left with the carriage. Setting out on foot with a crowd behind him, he was persuaded to accept the sheriff's protection, and the sheriff kept him in the jail building until morning before sending him to Wilmington. The Smyrna Times added that men who regarded him as a traitor to his race lay in wait for him on his way back to Wilmington, but its account breaks off at that point.

The Smyrna Times reported that police arrested seven men while the thrower escaped, whereas Every Evening said a party of white men rushed toward the assailants but could not find them. No report of charges or a trial appears in the coverage. The Wilmington Daily Gazette later wrote that Harris had also been mobbed at Wilmington and beaten at Chester, Pennsylvania, and blamed Republicans for all three.

Most papers learned of the attack from a one-sentence special dispatch to the New York Herald, dated Wilmington, August 2, which the Washington Evening Star printed that day under "Stoning a Colored Democrat." On August 3 it ran in the Wilmington Daily Gazette as "Free Speech in Delaware" and in the Richmond Dispatch as "Outrage on a Colored Virginia Democrat." Weeklies including the New Hampshire Patriot, the Weekly Floridian and the Point Pleasant Weekly Register reprinted it through mid-August.

The dispatch named no attackers, and distant Democratic papers supplied them: the Spirit of the Age in Vermont and the Orangeburg Democrat blamed "a Republican mob," and the Eureka Daily Sentinel "the Republican negroes of the city." In Oregon the State Rights Democrat headed the dispatch "An Omitted Dispatch" and charged that the Republican agent sending news to the Pacific coast had suppressed it.

The Richmond Dispatch reprinted the Every Evening narrative under the headline "Colored Bulldozers," and the Delaware State Journal, in "Our Delaware Bulldozers," defended Harris's right to speak whatever his character and accused local Republicans of indifference to an attack "right at our very doors." The Smyrna Times, by contrast, mocked Harris as the colored "orator" and told the attack as a comic scene.

The Delaware accounts placed the attack among Black members of the crowd, the State Journal saying Harris was "mobbed by a crowd of negroes," while distant Democratic papers called the attackers a Republican mob. The Spirit of the Age also said Harris was "driven out of town," whereas the wire and Every Evening said he took the sheriff's protection and left for Wilmington the next morning.

reader.title: Stoning of John H. Harris at New Castle, Delaware
bases: Stones and a brick were thrown from a crowd at a Black speaker, wounding a bystander, and he had to take refuge with the sheriff (A2, A8, A11); no one was killed.

The wire dispatch (A2) and three Delaware accounts (A7, A8, A11) agree that missiles were thrown at Harris at New Castle and that a white bystander was hurt; they differ on detail, not on the core event.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch (N. Y. Herald, from Wilmington)
accounts.gist: Harris tried to speak at New Castle Saturday night, was stoned, and had to seek the sheriff's protection; attackers not named.

accounts.label: Wilmington Every Evening (via Richmond Dispatch)
accounts.gist: A mostly Black crowd grew restless at his Democratic speech; a one-pound stone missed him and wounded McNulty; he was later persuaded to accept the sheriff's protection and stayed in the jail building overnight.

accounts.label: Smyrna Times
accounts.gist: A brick thrown by a Black man who escaped struck a white bystander; police arrested seven men; men who saw Harris as a traitor to his race lay in wait for him on his way back to Wilmington.

accounts.label: Delaware State Journal editorial
accounts.gist: Harris was mobbed by a crowd of Black men and a brick wounded a white listener; he had a right to speak for either party.

accounts.label: Democratic papers elsewhere
accounts.gist: Harris was stoned by a 'Republican mob' and forced out or into the sheriff's protection.

framing.detail: The dispatch ran under heads such as 'Stoning a Colored Democrat', 'Free Speech in Delaware' and 'Outrage on a Colored Virginia Democrat'.
The Delaware State Journal called it a 'deliberate attempt at bulldozing a negro' and charged Republicans with indifference.
The Smyrna Times ridiculed Harris as a colored 'orator' and swindler and called Delaware Democracy a white man's party, while reporting the attack and arrests.
Southern and Western Democratic papers used it partisanly: 'Republican mob', 'Southern outrages still continue', a suppressed dispatch.
